(CNN)  -- Manny Pacquiao's two-round demolition of Ricky Hatton has set up the prospect of the biggest money-spinning fight in the history of boxing. Pacquiao lands a solid right to Hatton on his way to a comprehensive victory. The Filipino knocked out the plucky but outclassed Briton in Las Vegas on Saturday night -- earning him by a conservative estimate at least $2 million dollars per minute. Hatton, who could well now hang up his gloves, will pocket more than $8 million as a consolation. Pacquiao's all-action style is popular with boxing followers and in his native Philippines the theaters which screened his fight live with Hatton were sold out well in advance with a ferocious demand for tickets. But the really big money lies in the Pay Per View (PPV) revenues generated by the U.S. Home Box Office (HBO) network. USA Today reported Monday that early indications from cable companies were that the scheduled 12-round light-welterweight bout could get as many as two million buys. Co-promoter Bob Arum was delighted with the figures especially as initial estimates were suggesting about one million boxing fans would shell out their cash. "We know based on those early numbers and based on experience the event will perform extremely well. If I had to guess, anywhere between 1.6 million and two million homes, which is a home run," he said. The record for a PPV event is the 2.4 million buys for 'Golden Boy' Oscar De La Hoya's May 2007 fight with Floyd Mayweather Jr., which generated a staggering $134 million in revenue. Mayweather, who also beat Hatton in another 'superfight' at the back end of 2007, astutely chose Saturday night in Vegas to announce he was coming out of retirement. Mayweather, nicknamed 'money' because of the enormous revenues he generates, will face Mexico's Juan Manuel Marquez on July 18 in his return to the ring. But the talk of the boxing world is an eventual match up against Pacquiao with the notional pound for pound title at stake as well as a massive pay day. "If Mayweather wants a piece of the 'little Filipino', just be my guest," Arum said before the dust had barely settled on the Hatton fight. With the flamboyant De La Hoya retired after being handed a painful beating by Pacquiao at the back end of 2008, the mantle of PPV king is set to fall to one of the two men who ended his ring career. Despite the global recession, the appetite for top prize fighting remains strong, but it is the more flamboyant characters who draw the biggest audiences. Last November's HBO clash between former pound for pound champion Roy Jones Jr. and the brilliant undefeated Welsh world champion Joe Calzaghe drew less than 250,000 buys. The only potential obstacle to a Pacquiao-Mayweather bout, the dangerous Marquez aside, is the relative sizes of the two men. Mayweather is a natural welterweight and would want a fight at 147 pounds, with Pacquiao, who started his remarkable career at light-flyweight, wanting the match at a lower weight. But big business and money is set to talk and many predict the showdown will come late this year, almost certainly in Las Vegas.

The victory marks Pacquiao's second consecutive statement win in as many weight divisions, having demolished Oscar De La Hoya last December before the Golden Boy retired. It cements the Filipino congressman-slash-boxer's status as arguably the biggest draw in the sport not named Mayweather — and now, the pressure mounts on Mayweather to answer boxing's biggest remaining question.

## The Mayweather Factor

Mayweather, who retired undefeated in 2008 but has flirted with a comeback, watched the carnage from ringside alongside promoter Bob Arum's rivals at Golden Boy Promotions. His presence did little to quiet speculation that a Pacquiao-Mayweather superfight is not just possible, but inevitable.

"Manny Pacquiao is a great fighter, one of the best in the world," Mayweather told reporters afterward, offering measured praise while sidestepping direct questions about a potential matchup. "We'll see what happens."

"This is the fight that has to happen," said HBO analyst Larry Merchant. "Manny Pacquiao just did to Ricky Hatton in six minutes what Floyd Mayweather couldn't do in twelve rounds. The whole boxing world is going to demand this fight."

At 30 years old, Pacquiao has now won world titles in six different weight classes, an achievement that already places him among the sport's all-time greats. "Manny is getting better every fight," Roach said. "The power, the speed, the boxing IQ — it's all coming together at the same time. I don't think there's a fighter alive right now who wants to see him across the ring."

For Hatton, the loss represents a crushing setback in a career that had been defined by working-class grit and rabid fan support. The 30-year-old Manchester native, making the walk in front of thousands of traveling British fans who turned the MGM Grand into a sea of blue and white, offered no excuses.

"He's just too good," Hatton said quietly at the post-fight press conference, an ice pack pressed to his face. "I've never been hit like that in my life."

## What's Next

Arum, never one to shy from hyperbole, wasted no time framing the endgame.

"Manny Pacquiao is now the biggest star in this sport," Arum declared. "Floyd Mayweather can talk all he wants, but every fan, every network, every promoter in the world knows what fight they want to see next."

With Pacquiao's stock never higher, the pressure now shifts squarely to Mayweather's camp to make the fight fans have wanted for years — a bout that could shatter pay-per-view records and settle, once and for all, who truly reigns supreme in the sport of boxing.

# The Business of Boxing: Pacquiao's Triumph Opens Doors to Boxing's Biggest Payday

Manny Pacquiao's demolition of Ricky Hatton has done more than cement his legacy as one of the sport's must-see attractions—it has reignited boxing's most lucrative hypothetical matchup and thrown into sharp relief the complex business calculations that now define the sport at its highest levels.

## A Statement Beyond the Scorecard

When Pacquiao dispatched Hatton in devastating fashion, he didn't just win a fight—he made a statement to promoters, networks, and the boxing world that he remains the sport's biggest draw and most dangerous fighter across multiple weight classes. The performance was emphatic enough to silence any lingering doubts about his ability to perform at the highest level against elite competition.

But in modern boxing, dominance in the ring is only half the equation. The other half is negotiation, positioning, and the intricate business machinery that determines whether superfights actually happen.

## The Mayweather Question

Inevitably, all roads lead back to Floyd Mayweather Jr. The pound-for-pound debate has hovered over both fighters' careers for years, and Pacquiao's victory has only intensified public and media pressure for the fight to materialize. Yet the path to making this fight happen is littered with obstacles that have nothing to do with either man's skill in the ring.

**Weight Class Complications**

One of the thorniest issues facing a potential Pacquiao-Mayweather bout is the question of catch weight. Pacquiao has built his legend by moving up in weight class after weight class, adding size and strength while somehow retaining his speed and power—an almost unprecedented career arc in boxing history.

Mayweather, meanwhile, has historically fought closer to the lower weight limits, and his camp has been vocal about wanting any potential bout contested at a weight that doesn't disadvantage their fighter. This has led to speculation about catch-weight arrangements—a contracted weight that sits between the fighters' preferred fighting weights—which historically have been a sticking point in high-profile negotiations.

These negotiations aren't merely technical footnotes; they represent legitimate competitive advantages. A few pounds can mean the difference between a fighter feeling comfortable and powerful versus drained and compromised. Every pound negotiated becomes leverage, and every leverage point becomes a potential dealbreaker.

## The Promotional Chess Match

Beyond weight, the business complexities multiply. Pacquiao and Mayweather have historically been aligned with different promotional entities and broadcast partners, meaning any fight requires unprecedented cooperation between parties that don't always see eye to eye. Revenue splits, undercard control, venue selection, and pay-per-view distribution all become negotiating points that can derail talks before fighters even discuss contract terms.

There's also the matter of legacy positioning. Both camps understand that this fight, whenever it happens, will be viewed as the defining bout of the era—perhaps of a generation. That magnitude raises the stakes on every point of negotiation, as neither side wants to enter the fight with a perceived disadvantage that could be pointed to afterward, win or lose.

## What Pacquiao's Win Really Means for Boxing's Economics

From a pure business perspective, Pacquiao's victory over Hatton likely increased his value in any future negotiation. Impressive wins translate directly into stronger positioning at the bargaining table—networks pay premiums for fighters who deliver both action and results, and promoters gain leverage when their fighter is the one whose stock is rising rather than declining.

This win also reinforces the narrative arc that makes Pacquiao commercially magnetic: the underdog story, the multiple-weight-class dominance, the crossover appeal beyond hardcore boxing fans. These are the elements that translate into pay-per-view buys, and they matter as much to promoters as tape-measure jabs and knockout power.

## The Road Ahead

Whether or not Pacquiao-Mayweather ultimately happens, the business lessons from this moment in boxing extend beyond one potential superfight. They illustrate how modern boxing operates at the intersection of athletic achievement and commercial strategy, where a dominant performance in the ring is merely the opening move in a much longer game of leverage, timing, and negotiation.

For fight fans, the frustration is real: the sport's biggest fights often get delayed or derailed by business considerations that have nothing to do with what happens between the ropes. But for those who understand boxing's economic ecosystem, these negotiations are simply the price of admission for matchups big enough to transcend the sport itself.

As speculation continues to swirl about a potential Pacquiao-Mayweather bout, one thing remains certain: the business of making this fight happen may prove just as complex and hard-fought as the fight itself would be.
